events.title: Emily Jacobs - New frontiers in women's brain health
events.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
New frontiers in women's brain health
Abstract
Gonadal hormones are potent neuromodulators of learning and memory. Yet, how these tiny molecules shape the structural and functional architecture of the human brain is virtually unknown. Many brain imaging studies miss a central feature of the endocrine system: hormone production ebbs and flows over time. Precision imaging allows us to map the mammalian brain with exquisite temporal resolution. Following individuals across major endocrine transitions, like the circadian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy, these studies reveal the human brain's capacity for rapid reorganization and hormones' role in shaping this process.
Jacobs' talk also considers why women’s health research is decades behind where it should be. Nowhere is this knowledge gap more visible than in neuroscience, where fewer than 0.5% of brain imaging articles focus on female-specific experiences, including menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause, that shape the lives of half the global population (Jacobs Nature 2023). Progress in women’s health will require a global shift in science culture, and that shift has started. Jacobs will examine emerging research programs, public policy changes, and private sector funding opportunities that are shining a floodlight on women’s health, and by doing so are opening up new frontiers for understanding health and disease.

Emily Jacobs, PhD
Professor Jacobs, University of California, Santa Barbara
Emily Jacobs is a Professor of Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara and Director of the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative. Her body of research examines dynamic endocrine modulation of the nervous system. In 2024 her team published the first detailed view of the human brain across pregnancy and she leads several multi-center studies on neurological changes tied to menopause. Prior to UCSB, she held a faculty appointment at Harvard Medical School and the Department of Medicine/Division of Women's Health at Brigham & Women's Hospital. She serves on the Steering Committee of the Coalition for Women’s Brain Health, the Milken Institute’s Women’s Health Network, the Foundation for Women’s Health, and the WHAM Research Collaborative to drive the national and international agenda on women’s health research. In recognition of her work, she was named a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Health and Society Scholar, a National Institutes of Health Women's Health Fellow, a National Academy of Sciences Frontiers of Science Kavli Fellow and Science News’ “Top 10 Scientists” to watch. Outside of the lab, Dr. Jacobs’ team partners with K-12 groups to advance girls' representation in STEM. You can find her work in the The New York Times, National Geographic, Scientific American, NPR, BBC, TED, Radiolab, Netflix, and MasterClass. She is a graduate of Smith and UC Berkeley.

events.title: Challenging the Archives: Reconstructing the Lives and Networks of Sex Workers in Early Modern Venice through Digital Tools
events.description:
In early modern Venice, sex workers were frequently accused of practicing magic and witchcraft, subsequently facing trial before the Holy Office. Drawing upon this empirical evidence, this project examines hundreds of Inquisition files spanning the years 1580 to 1630 to reconstruct these women's social networks. The objective is to contextualize and interpret the complex interrelationships between magic, sex work, and gender dynamics in early modern society. Adopting a microhistorical approach that integrates close reading with social network analysis and Gephi visualizations, this paper presents preliminary findings and discusses the methodological challenges of translating archival sources into digital data—particularly when researching the lives of marginalized, working-class women.

About the Speaker

Alessandra Celati is a research fellow in Early Modern History at the University of Turin, Italy. She earned her PhD from the University of Pisa and was a Marie Curie Global Fellow between Stanford University and the University of Verona, where she conducted research for several years. She is currently working on a project focused on "Love Magic and Sex Work in Early Modern Venice: A Network of Women in the Inquisition Records." For years, her research has focused on religious dissent, heretical movements, and witchcraft in the early modern period. She has integrated these topics using an interdisciplinary approach that combines religious history, women's history and the application of Digital Humanities tools. She has published numerous articles on these subjects in both Italian and international peer-reviewed journals.

Her first book, The World of Girolamo Donzellini: A Network of Heterodox Physicians in Sixteenth-Century Venice, was published by Routledge in 2023. In 2025, her second book, Donne che creano disordine. Storia di Caterina ed altre eretiche nel Cinquecento (Women Creating Disorder: The Story of Caterina and Other Heretics in the Sixteenth Century), was published in Einaudi's history series. The book is currently being translated into English, and this English version is under evaluation by Stanford University press.

events.title: The Gatekeepers: Hamburg, Germany and the Making of the Modern World
events.description:
The Gatekeepers is a history of the relationship between liberalism and globalization told through Hamburg, the city known as Germany’s “gateway to the world.” It tells the story of this city’s upper stratum, a wide-ranging but remarkably durable network of people and institutions centered on Hamburg but spiraling out into the world. For one century, this network committed itself to pulling Germany into the world economy and to pulling the promises of an interconnected world into Germany—yet also to wielding the power to determine what it meant to be open to the world. As they did so, Hamburg’s gatekeepers laid key foundations for the postwar Federal Republic of Germany’s foreign affairs and the architecture of post-1945 world order.

Join the Modern Europe Workshop in learning more about and discussing Jack Guenther's upcoming work. RSVP here for lunch.

Jack H. Guenther received his Ph.D. in history from Princeton in 2024. He specializes in German history and the history of capitalism, liberalism, and international order. His first book, The Gatekeepers: Hamburg, Germany, and the Making of the Modern World, is under contract with Yale University Press. His other research and writing have appeared in Archiv für Sozialgeschichte, Central European History, The English Historical Review, German History, H-Diplo, História Econômica & História de Empresas, and in edited volumes on Germany’s export economy and contemporary European foreign affairs.

events.title: Policed: A Latinx History of State Violence
events.description:
Spanning the nineteenth century to the present, Policed: A Latinx History of State Violence, examines how policing became a key component in the formation of Latinx identity and political consciousness, and still lies at the heart of many pressing issues confronting Latinx communities today, including immigration, employment, health, and housing. More than simply telling a story of police brutality and harassment, Marisol LeBrón powerfully shows that Latinx people have continually resisted state violence and worked to build a more liberated future.

Join the Global Studies in Migration and Diaspora Workshop in learning more about and discussing LeBrón's forthcoming book. The event will take place at Stanford Humanities Center (Board Room). RSVP here for lunch.

Marisol LeBrón is an Associate Professor of Critical Race and Ethnic Studies at the University of California, Santa Cruz. An interdisciplinary scholar, LeBrón’s research and teaching focus on social inequality, policing, violence, and protest. She is the author of Against Muerto Rico: Lessons from the Verano Boricua (2021) and Policing Life and Death: Race, Violence, and Resistance in Puerto Rico (2019). LeBrón is an active contributor to popular conversations about policing as well as Puerto Rico and its diaspora. She has published op-eds in The Washington Post, The Guardian and Truthout and has been interviewed by a number of news outlets. Dr. LeBrón is one of the co-creators and project leaders for the "Puerto Rico Syllabus" (#PRsyllabus), a digital resource for understanding the Puerto Rican debt crisis.

events.description:
Today's seminar features two talks from MBCT Student Members, Stanford PhD Students Elizabeth Jun and Lavonna Mark
Join our mailing list for MBCT Seminar announcements and updates about future events

Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex
Abstract
Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically.
To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts.

Meet the Speaker
Elizabeth Jun, PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University
Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit.

events.title: Superintelligence or Super Stupidity? Designing AI Systems for Human Flourishing
events.description:
Join the Tech Impact and Policy Center on November 3rd from 12PM–1PM Pacific for a seminar with Pat Pataranutaporn.

Stanford affiliates are invited to join us at 11:40 AM for lunch, prior to the seminar. The Fall Seminar Series continues through December; see our Fall Seminar Series page for speakers and topics. Sign up for our newsletter for announcements.

About the Seminar:

As AI becomes woven into our daily lives and social institutions, we are becoming “cyborgs,” extending our minds and capabilities through technology. But greater technological capability does not automatically lead to greater human flourishing. How can we design AI that strengthens our ability to learn, create, connect, and make thoughtful decisions? In this talk, I will introduce an interdisciplinary approach to building AI systems and studying their effects on people. Through personalized AI prototypes and large-scale experiments, my research explores how AI can both enhance and undermine human decision-making, well-being, relationships, and sense of self. This work combines design, engineering, and qualitative and quantitative research to advance a science of human-AI interaction grounded in human flourishing. I will also explore how research can translate into real-world impact: from an AI digital twin that supports long-term thinking and has reached users in more than 100 countries, to research that has helped shape legislation protecting children from companion AI. Finally, I will discuss our efforts with collaborators across academia, industry, and government to develop the first open benchmark for AI’s impact on people. Together, these projects offer lessons for connecting technical innovation with evidence, public policy, and meaningful social change.

About the Speaker:

Pat Pataranutaporn, PhD is an assistant professor, technologist, and researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he is the founding director of the Cyborg Psychology research group. He also serves as co-director of the MIT Media Lab Advancing Humans with AI (AHA) Research Program.

His research lies at the intersection of AI and human-computer interaction, where he focuses on inventing, investigating, and inspiring next-generation human-AI systems for human flourishing, applying insights from human psychology to AI and understanding how AI impacts human psychology.

As founding director of the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, he leads a team of interdisciplinary researchers to develop and study how AI can both augment and diminish human learning, decision-making, critical thinking, creativity, and other critical dimensions of human experience. His group is among the first to investigate emerging phenomena through empirical studies examining how AI reshapes cognition, emotion, and behavior, from emotional dependence on AI companions and cognitive manipulation to false memory implantation, placebo effects of human-AI interaction, and the co-evolution of human and machine intelligence.

His research has been translated into real-world impact, ranging from Future You, a widely adopted AI digital twin for supporting long-term thinking that has been used in over 100 countries worldwide, to research that has shaped legislation protecting children from companion AI, and leading efforts to develop the first open benchmark for the human impact of AI in collaboration with leaders across academia, industry, and government.

Pataranutaporn’s research contributions have been published in numerous peer-reviewed journals and conference proceedings, including ACM SIGCHI venues (CHI, IUI, DIS, ISWC, and AHs), ACM SIGGRAPH, NeurIPS, ICML, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Nature Machine Intelligence, Nature Biotechnology, Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), and New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM AI).

His work has been highlighted by the United Nations AI for Good forum and featured in Technology Review, the New York Times, the Guardian, Bloomberg, the Washington Post, Forbes, the Atlantic, Scientific American, the Wall Street Journal, and more. His work has also been honored as one of TIME’s “Best Inventions of 2023” and was included in Fast Company’s “2023 World Changing Ideas.”

Pataranutaporn has collaborated with researchers from both academia and industry, including teams from NASA, Stanford Medicine, Harvard, Mass General Brigham, UCSB, UCLA, UC Irvine, Microsoft Research, OpenAI, NTT Data, KBTG, and more.

He serves as an advisor to the Psychology of Technology Institute and Partnership on AI. He also served as co-creator and writer of the Netflix sci-fi anthology series Tomorrow and I, which premiered in 2024.

events.description:
Lunch Club provides affiliates of the Stanford Archaeology Center with a community-oriented forum for engagement with current issues in archaeology. On Nov 4, 2026, we will host Dr.Jon Daehnke from University of California, Santa Cruz.

Abstract:

In this talk I explore the contested nature of marking Indigenous history and continued presence/absence in settler colonial states. Specifically, I look at monuments, memorials, and other sites of public history and heritage along the Columbia River that offer reminders of Indigenous – and in this case, specifically Chinook – occupation of the landscape. In part, this work addresses the challenges that the Chinook Indian Nation faces regarding the public representation of their own history, especially at “official” sites of heritage. But centrally in the work I explore how the Chinook are responding to, and actively shaping, discussions and practice surrounding monuments, memorials, and sites of heritage. In part this is through increased participation in management of “official” sites of heritage. But it is also connected to the role that the revitalization of Chinookan art has played in reclaiming heritage landscapes, as well as opportunities for the Chinook to tell their own stories on their own lands.

events.title: DAAAS Movie Night: The Eyes of Ghana
events.description:
Dear Community,

Please join DAAAS Movie Nights for the screening of THE EYES OF GHANA. This is an American documentary feature film directed by Ben Proudfoot and executive produced by Barack and Michelle Obama, Higher Ground Media. The film follows Chris Hesse, the personal cameraman to revolutionary leader Kwame Nkrumah, the first president of Ghana, who was deposed in a coup d'état in 1966. Having saved over 1,000 rolls of film from Nkrumah's enemies who sought to destroy them, Hesse, now in his 90's, passes them on to a protégé and together they attempt to hold a public screening of footage never seen in public before. The film screening will be followed by a conversation with one of the film's producers, Nana Adwoa Frimpong facilitated by DAAAS's award-winning Professor Aaron Van Jordan.

About the Film

Kwame Nkrumah was the first president of Ghana and a key figure in Africa’s liberation movement. Nkrumah was also a great lover of cinema and recognised the extraordinary political power of the moving image. To this end, he set up cinemas all around Ghana, while ensuring that his every move was documented on film, courtesy of his personal cinematographer Chris Hesse, who—together with clips from the vast archive he shot—forms the vibrant centre of this delightful film. The Eyes of Ghana is an extraordinary document, not just of Nkrumah’s life and Ghana’s independence, but also of a 20th century that is starting to fade from view, even as its events continue to cascade like dominoes into our current age. A deeply felt love letter to the power of cinema, both as an art form and store of historical record, the film is a must-see for anyone with a devotional love for film.

events.title: Cristopher Niell - Neural circuits for natural vision
events.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
Neural circuits for natural vision
Abstract
Natural visual processing entails a complex interplay between sensory input, behavioral context, and on-going brain dynamics. Our lab seeks to understand how these processes give rise to goal-directed visual behaviors, by exploring the neural circuits mediating ethologically relevant behaviors that laboratory mice perform, including prey capture and distance estimation. We are also implementing novel experimental approaches to investigate neural coding of the visual scene as animals freely move through their environment. Finally, I will present a new research direction studying the completely different, yet largely unexplored, visual system of the octopus.In this work, we are elucidating both the functional and cell type organization to identify both shared and novel aspects of visual computation.
Cristopher Niell
University of Oregon
Cristopher Niell received his B.S. in physics at Stanford University, doing research in single-molecule biophysics with Dr. Steven Chu. He then remained at Stanford to obtain his PhD with Dr. Stephen Smith, studying the development and function of the zebrafish visual system. He then moved to UCSF to perform post-doctoral study with Dr. Michael Stryker, where he initiated studies of visual processing and behavioral state in the mouse cortex. He established his lab at University of Oregon in 2011, where he is now a Full Professor in the Department of Biology and Institute of Neuroscience. His lab uses a combination of neural recording and imaging methods, operant and ethological behaviors, and computational analysis to study the neural circuits that underlie visually guided behavior and perception.

events.title: Historical Architecture in Disaster Zones: Digital Documentation, Archiving, and Preservation
events.description:
This talk present a project that works in an international, collaborative research setting to gather data - photographs from the nineteenth century to the present, scholarly literature, oral histories, maps and plans—to document historical monuments affected by the February 2023 earthquakes in Turkey and Syria. The project is focusing on the city of Antakya, where monuments dating from the Roman period to the Ottoman Empire, from 300 BCE to the nineteenth century, ranging from commercial buildings to churches, mosques, and synagogues were heavily damaged or destroyed by the earthquakes. This talk will present initial versions of virtual tours through monuments and neighborhoods, as well as the website based on an OCHRE database, to be launched in early 2027.

About the Speakers

Patricia Blessing is Associate Professor of Art History at Stanford University. Blessing is the author of Rebuilding Anatolia after the Mongol Conquest: Islamic Architecture in the Lands of Rūm, 1240–1330 (Ashgate, 2014) and Architecture and Material Politics in the Fifteenth-century Ottoman Empire (Cambridge University Press, 2022). With Elizabeth Dospel Williams and Eiren Shea, she co-authored Medieval Textiles across Eurasia, c. 300-1400 for the Cambridge Elements series Global Middle Ages (Cambridge University Press, 2023). Bryant Lin, MD, MEng is a primary care physician, educator and researcher. events.title: Daniel Wurgaft | A Resource Rational Analysis of Representations: Geometry, Inference, Capacity
events.description:
Abstract

Neural systems process information by forming representations of the world. Studies of representational geometry have revealed remarkably structured representations in biological and artificial systems, as well as surprising alignment in representations across systems. Why do representations across systems converge to similar structures, how do these structures encode concepts and uncertainty over them, and how are they shaped by resource constraints?

Here, we tackle these questions in neural networks through the lens of resource rationality, asking what representations are optimal for solving a task, given dimensionality and linear readout constraints. We derive a notion of optimal linear representations, and show that these emerge across varied architectures and tasks, providing a simple explanation for representational convergence as alignment toward the optimal solution. This shared treatment motivates a normative formalization of conceptual spaces that generalizes the linear representation hypothesis. We then extend this account to uncertainty and inference over conceptual spaces, asking how representations should change in response to in-context evidence, and finally to resource-constrained settings involving representational interference.

About the Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series

The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science.

As neuroscience continues to generate vast amounts of data—from intricate neural circuit maps to large-scale brain activity recordings—the need for interdisciplinary expertise in data science, statistics, and engineering has never been more critical.

The Center for Neural Data Science mission is to advance brain research through the development of cutting-edge analytical methodologies and collaborative approaches. Stanford's affiliates are invited to join this vibrant community dedicated to transformative discoveries.

events.title: A Rift in Time. Reinhart Koselleck and the Theory of History
events.description:
What possible futures does history contain? Reinhart Koselleck has become one the most widely read and cited twentieth-century German historians and theorists of history, not just for the new field of “global conceptual history” but essentially for anyone across disciplines writing about questions of time, temporality, and historical thought. Yet the recent uptick of interest in his work as part of the “temporal turn” obscures the fact that Koselleck was working throughout his life on something even more ambitious: a new theory of history or rather a theory of the conditions of possible histories, and hence possible futures, written by an historian in an age of catastrophes.

Based on a wealth of previously inaccessible archival materials, this talk explores Koselleck’s critique of the modern concept of History and what he called its “temporalization”—from Critique and Crisis to his essays on dreams and war memorials—and parses out his parallel search for an antidote in the form of a new theory of historical knowledge, most visible in his late essay collection Sediments of Time. We will ask what remains of Koselleck’s theoretical reckoning with ruptured time and repetition in history and whether it can be untangled from the experiences of loss and complicity of his generation.

Join the Modern Europe Workshop in learning more about and discussing Stefan-Ludgwig Hoffman's research. RSVP for refreshments.

Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann is Chancellor’s Professor of History at the University of California, Berkeley. His most recent book, Der Riss in der Zeit. Kosellecks ungeschriebene Historik (Suhrkamp, 2023), will come out in English translation with Princeton UP in September 2027. Currently, he is working on two projects: a book-length essay on human rights internationalism from imperial beginnings to the present polycrises, and a monograph on everyday life in Berlin in the 1940s, as the city went from multinational capital of the Nazi Empire to shattered metropolis of the early Cold War. His previous two books traced the afterlives of Enlightenment concepts and social practices (sociability, humanity, cosmopolitanism, civil society) in the long nineteenth century and their late twentieth-century resurgence. Together with Samuel Moyn, he is the editor of the Cambridge series Human Rights in History.

events.title: BOOK LAUNCH: Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland
events.description:
The Department of African and African American Studies (DAAAS) in collaboration with the Center for South Asia (CSA) cordially invite the Stanford Community for a special book launch!

We are excited to celebrate the publication of a new book by our visiting postdoctoral scholar, Danny Shanhan, Ph.D titled, Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland.

This book is the first substantial study of emergency law's relationship to literature in either the Northern Irish or the Kashmiri conflict and develops an original legal history that links these laws to a shared British colonial root. Engaging a wide range of fiction, poetry and film, from canonical poets Seamus Heaney and Agha Shahid Ali to contemporary works by Anna Burns, Mirza Waheed, and Bollywood filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj, the book examines the literary response to the suspension of normative legal rights such as habeas corpus, the right to silence and even, in Kashmir, the right to life. By bringing these literary cultures together for the first time, it develops a literary and legal history that reveals common roots in colonial-era jurisprudence. The book re-situates these corpora, often isolated in scholarly work, as important parts of the global, material legacies of colonialism.

Join us for an evening of conversation, community and celebration and Danny shares his work. This will be followed by a discussion and Q&A with Roanne Kantor, Assistant Professor of English.

About the Seminar:

Extensive attention has been paid to the potential harms of media consumption generally, and social media use in particular, with relatively little consideration given to the potential psychological benefits of media use. This talk will address why this bias exists and its potential for unintended negative consequences. Evidence of how self-selected and prescribed digital media content can support desirable outcomes, including reduced stress and procrastination, increased goal motivation and pursuit, and increased empathy and relational satisfaction, will be shared to highlight the need for better understanding of how to empower users to make media choices that can support their psychological well-being.

About the Speaker:

Robin L. Nabi is a Professor of Communication at the University of California, Santa Barbara. With degrees from Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania, she has published over 100 journal articles and book chapters investigating the effects of media use on emotional experiences, decision-making, and well-being. She is the co-editor of two volumes: The SAGE Handbook of Media Processes and Effects and Emotions in the Digital World (Oxford University Press). She is a Fellow of the International Communication Association, and her research has been featured in numerous media outlets, including the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, USA Today, NPR, CBC/Radio-Canada, and the Harvard Business Review.

events.title: A Conversation with Researchers: Tracking HIV Through Wastewater in South Africa
events.description:
Wastewater surveillance helped track COVID-19. Can it do the same for HIV?

The King Center on Global Development welcomes four visiting researchers from the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC), working on HIV wastewater surveillance in KwaZulu-Natal.

A joint Stanford-SAMRC team is mapping HIV concentrations across northern KwaZulu-Natal to detect unrecognized transmission of HIV, measure changes in drug resistance and in anti-retroviral drug residues over time, enhance population surveillance, and track the success of interventions, offering a potentially cost-effective and relatively unbiased approach to public health monitoring.

Julie Parsonnet and Alexandra Boehm are co-Principal Investigators of the multiyear HIV Wastewater Epidemiology in South Africa Initiative.

Join Parsonnet and the SAMRC team for conversation over lunch, an opportunity to learn firsthand from African epidemiologists and laboratory scientists about the realities of their work in the field, and about infectious disease surveillance in vulnerable communities.

About the speakers:

Dr. Nomfundo Mahlangeni is a Senior Scientist at the SAMRC, where she leads the Water, Sanitation and Society Research Program within the Environment and Health Research Unit (EHRU). Her recent work includes detection and quantification of pharmaceutical compounds, including antiretroviral drugs, in wastewater. She is also passionate about research addressing the health and well-being of women and children in vulnerable communities.

Dr. Noluxabiso Mangwana is a Senior Scientist and epidemiologist at SAMRC’s Biomedical Research and Innovation Platform. Her research spans wastewater and environmental surveillance, antimicrobial resistance, and infectious disease epidemiology, integrating molecular tools and epidemiological analysis to inform public health action. Her current work includes infectious disease surveillance and the development of AMR surveillance within a One Health framework.

Nomacusi Sibeko is a Senior Research Technologist at SAMRC within the Environment and Health Research Unit (EHRU). Her research background includes microbiome–drug interactions, antimicrobial evaluations, and innovative approaches to water, urine, and faecal sludge treatment. In her current role, Sibeko is involved in environmental health research, particularly the wastewater-based surveillance of infectious diseases. She is passionate about applying laboratory science to address public health challenges.

Sthembile Sithole is a laboratory technician based at the University of Zululand, where she currently supports SAMRC on the Wastewater Surveillance of HIV RNA and Antiretroviral Drugs in KwaZulu-Natal, in collaboration with Stanford University. Her academic and research interests are focused on molecular and laboratory-based approaches to public health research, with particular interest in infectious disease surveillance and the application of wastewater epidemiology.

About the moderator:

Dr. Julie Parsonnet is a King Center faculty affiliate and Stanford Professor of Epidemiology and Population Health. Dr. Parsonnet is an Infectious Diseases clinician and epidemiologist whose research focuses on the role of infections in chronic disease. Her early work was pivotal in establishing H. pylori as a cause of gastric cancer and gastric lymphoma as well as protective effects of infections against esophageal diseases. She did extensive work on COVID during the pandemic, including surveillance of COVID in wastewater. More recently, she has expanded this work with Dr. Alexandra Boehm to study other viruses, including HIV.

events.title: Juan Gallego | More is different in neural populations
events.description:
Dr. Juan Gallego from the Champalimaud Foundation returns for the 2026–2027 MBCT Seminar Series
Join our mailing list for MBCT Seminar announcements and updates about future events

Abstract
Behaviour arises from interactions among regions and nuclei across the brain, each composed of a large number of interacting cells whose behaviour depends on complex interactions at the molecular level, and so on. The concept of emergence —“more is different”— says that new properties can arise from interactions among constituent parts that do not themselves have these properties. This most certainly applies to interactions among many brain regions, neurons, or molecules. Thus, the question arises: what level should we focus on if we want to understand how the brain generates behaviour?
In this talk, I will propose that the level of neural populations is appropriate to link specific brain functions to behavioural output. First, I will discuss evidence that studying the emergent properties of interacting neural populations leads to qualitatively new descriptions of brain function that are elusive when aggregating the individualistic behaviour of constituent neurons. Then, I will summarize evidence that the properties of this collective neural behaviour are not mere mathematical abstractions, but real patterns grounded in the biological substrates of the brain. I will end by discussing challenges and opportunities to further our understanding of brain function using this framework.

Continue the conversation: All attendees are invited to digest the seminar with a complimentary dinner with the speaker in the Theory Center after the seminar.

Meet the Speaker
Juan Gallego, Principal Investigator, Champalimaud Foundation
Hosted by Yiqi Jiang (Schnitzer Lab & Linderman Lab)
Dr. Juan Gallego is a Principal Investigator at the Champalimaud Foundation, which he joined in October 2025. Prior to that, he was an Associate Professor at Imperial College London (since 2020), and held Postdoctoral Fellowships at the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and Northwestern University. He was awarded a PhD from CSIC and University Carlos III in 2013.

Dr. Gallego’s research focuses on understanding how animals including humans acquire, execute and adapt their movements. To this end, his lab combines behavioural experiments in mice and humans, large-scale neural recordings, closed-loop manipulations, data analysis techniques, and computational models. He is also interested in applying his lab’s findings to advance neurotechnologies to restore function to people with movement disorders. During his career, he has published around fourty journal articles on these topics. His research has been funded by the EU Commission, the UK Research Institutes, ARIA, and the ERC.

events.title: Jonathan Kipnis - Navigating turbulent CNS waters
events.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
Navigating turbulent CNS waters
Abstract
The central nervous system was long viewed as an immune-privileged organ, largely isolated from peripheral physiology. Over the past decade, this paradigm has shifted. Our work has revealed that the brain continuously exchanges signals, cells, and molecules with the immune and lymphatic systems, and that these interactions are essential for normal brain function, aging, and disease. In this lecture, I will discuss recent discoveries that redefine the anatomical and physiological pathways connecting the brain to the rest of the body, including meningeal lymphatics, skull and vertebral bone marrow, and cerebrospinal fluid dynamics. I will also present emerging evidence that dysfunction of these systems contributes to neurological disorders and cognitive decline, highlighting new therapeutic opportunities at the interface of neuroscience and immunology.

Jonathan Kipnis, PhD
Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology, Washington University at St. Louis
Dr. Jonathan (Jony) Kipnis is BJC Investigator, Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology and Professor of Neurology, Neuroscience, and Neurosurgery at Washington University in St. Louis, School of Medicine. He is also the inaugural Director of Brain immunology and Glia (BIG) Center at Washington University. Jony graduated from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, where he was Sir Charles Clore Scholar and a recipient of distinguished prize for scientific achievements awarded by the Israeli Parliament, The Knesset.
The Kipnis laboratory investigates the interactions between the immune system and the central nervous system, with a focus on the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern brain function in health, aging, and neurological disease. His group demonstrated that normal brain function depends, in part, on an intact immune system and identified several cytokines as important neuromodulators. Most notably, his laboratory discovered the meningeal lymphatic vessels that drain the central nervous system into peripheral lymph nodes, revealing a direct anatomical link between the brain and the immune system. This finding reshaped the concept of central nervous system immune privilege and opened new avenues for studying neuroimmune interactions in health and disease, with implications for disorders including Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, autism, and age-related cognitive decline.
Dr. Kipnis is a member of National Academy of Medicine.

events.description:
This workshop is a part of the T. T. & W. F. Chao Buddhism and Contemporary Society Series and will explore the early Buddhist sources of mindfulness meditation in theory and in practice. Participants will be guided through an examination of the teachings that form the shared inheritance of all later Buddhist traditions and that also inform many contemporary applications. Throughout the day, we will be looking into multiple constructs and perspectives on mindfulness and their practical implications, discovering how theory, practice, and their interweaving have continually evolved—shaped by diverse maps and goals of the Buddhist path across time, through different cultures, and into present-day recontextualizations.

The workshop will offer participants the opportunity for experiential exploration of the relevant practices together with an accessible scholarly grounding in the primary textual sources in translation.

events.title: YoungJu Jo | Data-driven discovery and control of neural computations
events.description:
Abstract

The brain is a nonlinear dynamical system whose evolving population activity gives rise to computations that guide behavior. We will present a data-driven systems neuroscience framework that integrates large-scale neurophysiology, interpretable dynamical systems modeling, and targeted perturbations in cognitive animal models. This approach has enabled the discovery of cell-type-specific and brain-wide dynamical structures underlying reward and memory computations, including attractor manifolds that integrate past rewards and steer future decision-making. To enable causal tests and model-guided control of these computations, we have developed optical and genetic technologies for cellular-resolution, bidirectional control of neural populations, along with optimal control approaches for designing perturbations. Together, these converging advances set the stage for a closed-loop strategy to measure, model, and control neural dynamics and computations, toward the long-term vision of writing complex information into the brain.

Bio

YoungJu Jo is an Assistant Professor and the Brody Family Faculty Fellow in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute at the University of California, Berkeley. His laboratory develops and applies next-generation neurotechnologies to measure, model, and control neural dynamics and computations in behaving animals. He completed his postdoctoral training in Bioengineering in 2026, Ph.D. in Applied Physics in 2024, and M.S. in Biology in 2020, all at Stanford University, where he studied experimental and computational systems neuroscience with Profs. Karl Deisseroth, David Sussillo, and Krishna Shenoy. Before transitioning to neuroscience, he received his B.S. in Physics and Mathematics from KAIST in 2018, where he worked on computational imaging and optogenetics with Profs. YongKeun Park and Won Do Heo. His early work on AI-powered holographic microscopy was recognized with the 2022 Agarwal Award and commercialized by Tomocube.

About the Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series

The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science.

As neuroscience continues to generate vast amounts of data—from intricate neural circuit maps to large-scale brain activity recordings—the need for interdisciplinary expertise in data science, statistics, and engineering has never been more critical.

The Center for Neural Data Science mission is to advance brain research through the development of cutting-edge analytical methodologies and collaborative approaches. Stanford's affiliates are invited to join this vibrant community dedicated to transformative discoveries.

This seminar series is only offered in person.

events.title: Artist Salon: North African Traditions, New Music Creating a Concerto for Oud and Baroque Orchestra
events.description:
Join us for an Artist Salon: North African Traditions, New Music Creating a Concerto for Oud and Baroque Orchestra, a free public conversation presented by Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra & Chorale, Stanford Live, and Stanford's Department of African and African American Studies.

Discover the story of the oud—the fretless, pear-shaped lute whose sound has shaped musical traditions across North Africa and the Middle East for centuries and which is an ancestor of the modern guitar.

Composer Tarik O'Regan and oud virtuoso Joseph Tawadros will take audiences behind the scenes of a new piece O’Regan has composed for oud and Baroque orchestra, scheduled to premiere at Bing Concert Hall on February 7, 2027.

O'Regan, whose music has been performed by leading ensembles around the world, will discuss the inspiration behind the work, while Tawadros—whose performances have introduced international audiences to the expressive sound of the oud—will share the instrument's rich musical traditions, demonstrate its remarkable range, and offer insights into bringing this new composition to life. The conversation will be moderated by Stanford professor and acclaimed scholar Professor Matthew D. Morrison, whose work explores music, culture, and identity.

The event also features live musical demonstration by Joseph Tawadros, a performance by the Stanford Middle Eastern Ensemble, and an audience Q&A, offering attendees the opportunity to engage directly with the artists.

Date: Tuesday February 2, 2027

Time: 5-7pm

Location: Building 80 (Main Quad)

Light bites and refreshments will be served.

Admission is free, but RSVP is required as space is limited.

Join us at the concert on Sunday, February 7 at 2.30pm at Bing Concert Hall. Visit live.stanford.edu for tickets and more information.

Co-presented by the Center for African Studies, Department of Music, Institite for Diversity in the Arts, Middle Eastern Studies Forum and Sohaib and Sara Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies.

events.title: Distinguished Lecture Series Lunch Talk | From Plans to People: Rough-and-Ready Reconstructions of a Bronze Age Citadel
events.description:
Each quarter, the Stanford Archaeology Center invites prominent archaeologists from around the globe to be in residence for a week as a Distinguished Lecturer. During their residency, the Distinguished Lecturer gives two lectures and interacts with faculty, postdoctoral scholars and students. Stanford Archaeology Center will host Prof. Christopher H. Roosevelt from Koc University over two days (Feb 24 and Feb 25 for the Winter Quarter of this academic year.

Abstract:

Visual and numeric reconstructions of archaeological sites can become their most evocative and indelible portraits. A bird's-eye view or a population figure often conveys a palpable sense of an ancient community and outlives the data used to produce it. Because such reconstructions are so easily convincing and lasting, their resolution should match that of their underlying datasets. Yet the history of archaeology, from Çatalhöyük to Troy and beyond, is rife with disputed reconstructions and corrected population estimates. We should question not how accurate such reconstructions must be, but what resolution the evidence can honestly support.

Using recent work of the Kaymakçı Archaeological Project in western Anatolia, this lecture presents a combined approach to visual and numerical reconstructions of a second-millennium BCE citadel and its population that privileges the spatial and chronological resolution of its datasets over the photorealism or exactitude of its outputs. Aerial and ground-based remote sensing and surface survey of the site’s 9-hectare citadel, together with 2,500 square meters of excavation within it, inform a workflow of vector tracing, typological and certainty tagging, and metrical extrapolation from excavated data. The initial result is one of the most extensive reconstructions of urban fabric yet available for a Bronze Age site in the region. Treated as a palimpsest rather than a snapshot of a single point in time, that structured 2D plan then serves as the basis for a defensible range of population estimates and algorithmically generated 3D models of the citadel. Deliberately rough and ready, these visual and numerical reconstructions offer a holistic sense of the place and its people without claiming a precision the evidence cannot support.

She brings a deep love of art, storytelling, and community to her work, and believes that every artwork — and every person — holds a story worth sharing. No RSVP necessary, walk-ins welcome!
